title: Voltaic cells and cell notation
competency: Describe how a galvanic cell works, explain the salt bridge, compare galvanic and electrolytic cells, and write cell notation.

keywords.def: A cell in which a spontaneous redox reaction produces electricity (also voltaic cell).
A tube of inert electrolyte (KNO₃, KCl) that joins two half-cells and keeps them neutral.
anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode.

en.text: A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to make electricity. The two half-reactions happen in separate compartments, so electrons must flow through the external wire from the anode (oxidation, negative) to the cathode (reduction, positive). A salt bridge of inert ions keeps both solutions neutral and completes the circuit. The Daniell cell, Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu, gives 1.10 V.

screens.title: Zinc in copper sulfate
screens.ask: A zinc strip is dipped straight into blue CuSO₄ solution. What do you see?
opts: Copper coats the zinc and the blue fades, with no useful current
screens.after: Zn gives electrons directly to Cu²⁺. To get a current, the two must be separated.

screens.title: Building a galvanic cell
paras: A spontaneous redox reaction is split into two half-cells.
Daniell cell: Zn in ZnSO₄ and Cu in CuSO₄.
Anode (−): Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cathode (+): Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Electrons flow through the wire from Zn to Cu.

screens.title: The salt bridge
paras: An inverted U-tube of KNO₃ or KCl solution.
Anions move toward the anode compartment; cations toward the cathode compartment.
It keeps each solution neutral and completes the circuit.
Without it, charge builds up and the current stops.

screens.title: Galvanic or electrolytic?
paras: Both: oxidation at the anode, reduction at the cathode.

screens.text: Which statement about voltaic cells is NOT correct?
opts: Electrons flow from the cathode to the anode
screens.ans: Electrons flow from the cathode to the anode
screens.why: Electrons are made at the anode and used at the cathode: anode → cathode.

screens.text: In a galvanic cell, the anode is
screens.why: Electrons pile up where oxidation releases them. (In electrolysis the anode is positive.)

screens.text: What happens if the salt bridge is removed?
opts: Charge builds up and the current stops
screens.ans: Charge builds up and the current stops
screens.why: Zn²⁺ piles up in one beaker and SO₄²⁻ is left in the other; the circuit is broken.

en.text: Cell notation writes the anode on the left and the cathode on the right: anode | anode solution || cathode solution | cathode. A single line is a phase boundary, the double line is the salt bridge, commas separate species in one solution, and concentrations go in brackets. Inert electrodes such as Pt or graphite are written at the ends; salt-bridge and spectator ions are left out.

am.text: የሴል አጻጻፍ፡ አኖድ | የአኖድ መፍትሄ || የካቶድ መፍትሄ | ካቶድ። ነጠላ መስመር የደረጃ ወሰን፣ ድርብ መስመር የጨው ድልድይ ነው።

screens.title: Read the code
screens.ask: In Zn(s) | Zn²⁺(aq) || Cu²⁺(aq) | Cu(s), what does the double line || stand for?
screens.after: The double line is the salt bridge between the two half-cells; single lines are phase boundaries.

screens.title: Rules for cell notation
paras: Anode half-cell on the left, cathode on the right.
Single line |: boundary between phases (solid | solution).
Commas: species in the same solution.
Do not write salt-bridge or spectator ions.

screens.text: Al in 1 M Al(NO₃)₃ is joined to Ag in 1 M AgNO₃. The cell notation is
opts: Al(s) | Al³⁺(1 M) || Ag⁺(1 M) | Ag(s)
Ag(s) | Ag⁺(1 M) || Al³⁺(1 M) | Al(s)
screens.ans: Al(s) | Al³⁺(1 M) || Ag⁺(1 M) | Ag(s)
screens.why: Al (E° −1.66 V) is oxidized: it is the anode, written on the left. NO₃⁻ is a spectator.
